content: Saturated fat is a type of fat composed of triglycerides that contain only saturated fatty acids. These fatty acids lack double bonds between the carbon atoms in their chains, meaning they are fully saturated with hydrogen atoms. There are various naturally occurring saturated fatty acids, differing only in the number of carbon atoms in their chains, which can range from 1 to 24. Examples include butyric acid (4 carbon atoms, found in butter), lauric acid (12 carbon atoms, found in breast milk, coconut oil, and palm oil), myristic acid (14 carbon atoms, found in cow milk and dairy products), palmitic acid (16 carbon atoms, found in palm oil and meat), and stearic acid (18 carbon atoms, found in meat and cocoa butter). Fats derived from animals and plants, which are consumed as food, contain varying proportions of saturated and unsaturated fats. Foods high in saturated fat include butter, ghee, suet, tallow, lard, coconut oil, cottonseed oil, palm kernel oil, dairy products (especially cream and cheese), meat, and certain processed foods. Saturated fats, such as those in coconut oil and butter, are more solid at room temperature, more stable during cooking, and have longer shelf lives compared to oils like olive oil or other liquid vegetable oils. Hydrogenation of liquid vegetable oils increases their shelf life and makes them solid at room temperature, but these are not equivalent to pure, unadulterated saturated fats. Conversely, dehydrogenation processes convert saturated fats into unsaturated fats. The relationship between dietary fats and cardiovascular disease (CVD), particularly coronary heart disease (CHD), has been extensively studied. Evidence from animal experiments, observational studies, clinical trials, and metabolic studies in diverse populations consistently shows that saturated fatty acids increase total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels. Replacing saturated fatty acids with polyunsaturated fatty acids, such as linoleic acid, has been shown to reduce the risk of CHD. Large randomized clinical trials have demonstrated that substituting saturated and trans fats with polyunsaturated vegetable oils lowers the risk of CHD. Diets high in saturated fat are associated with an increased incidence of atherosclerosis and CHD in both animal and human studies. Controlled experimental studies have shown that high saturated fat intake leads to unfavorable changes in cholesterol profiles, which are predictors of heart attacks and other cardiovascular diseases. A 2003 meta-analysis published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition concluded that diets high in saturated fat negatively impact cholesterol profiles. Studies comparing control diets to Mediterranean diets, which replace saturated fats with monoand polyunsaturated fats, have shown significant reductions in the likelihood of secondary heart attacks, cardiac death, heart failure, or stroke. Epidemiological studies have also linked high consumption of saturated fatty acids, such as lauric, myristic, palmitic, and stearic acids, to a higher prevalence of CHD. Lauric acid, while a predictor of heart disease, may have a smaller impact compared to myristic and palmitic acids. The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified foods rich in lauric acid as a possible contributor to CHD. In 2004, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommended that Americans continue to reduce their intake of saturated fats. Similarly, the American Heart Association (AHA) advised limiting saturated fat intake to less than 7% of total daily calories in its 2006 guidelines. These recommendations align with those of the WHO and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which have concluded that reducing saturated fat consumption improves cholesterol profiles and reduces the risk of heart disease. However, some studies have reported conflicting findings. For example, research has shown that women who consumed higher amounts of saturated fats had less atherosclerotic plaque buildup in their arteries, healthier HDL-to-LDL cholesterol ratios, and more favorable blood serum levels of triglycerides and free fatty acids. Dr. Mary Enig, a biochemist and nutritionist, has argued that many studies fail to distinguish between saturated fats and trans fats. She also emphasizes that fats in foods are typically a mixture of saturated, monounsaturated, and polyunsaturated fats. According to Dr. Enig, saturated fats are essential for hormone production, cellular membrane stability, organ cushioning, and energy. Specific fatty acids, such as lauric, myristic, and palmitic acids, play critical roles in biochemical signaling processes, including G-protein receptor functions, which require lipid coupling for proper localization and function. Palmitic and myristic acids are involved in stabilization processes like palmitoylation and myristoylation, respectively. Myristic acid has also been linked to immune system function and tumor suppression. A deficiency in saturated fatty acids may lead to age-related declines in white blood cell function, immune dysfunction, and even cancer. Research conducted in the 1970s by Canadian scientists on rapeseed and canola oil suggested that at least 25% of dietary fat should be in the form of saturated fat. A 3-year study of 235 postmenopausal women found that higher saturated fat intake was associated with less progression of coronary atherosclerosis. Coronary angiography of 2,243 coronary artery segments revealed that greater consumption of polyunsaturated oils was associated with greater progression of atherosclerosis. A 2007 study of 297 Portuguese men who had experienced acute myocardial infarction (MI) found that total fat intake, as well as lauric, palmitic, and oleic acids, were inversely associated with acute MI. Low intake of total fat and lauric acid from dairy products was linked to acute MI. Some prospective studies suggest that replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats is more effective in reducing CHD risk than simply lowering total fat consumption. Dr. Enig has also highlighted the nutritional benefits of saturated fats. Lauric acid, a medium-chain fatty acid, has antimicrobial properties and serves as a precursor to monolaurin, an antimicrobial lipid. Lauric acid contributes to the antimicrobial properties of human breast milk and may be a conditionally essential fatty acid, as it cannot be synthesized by mammals other than lactating females and must be obtained through the diet. The lipid hypothesis, which posits that saturated fats cause heart disease, forms the basis of much of the concern surrounding saturated fat consumption. However, the history of saturated and trans fats complicates this narrative. Hydrogenated oils were once promoted as healthier alternatives to naturally occurring saturated fats. Critics, including Dr. Enig, have suggested that corporate interests played a role in the negative portrayal of saturated fats. Another issue is the formation of advanced glycation end products (AGEs) and oxidation products during cooking, which some studies have not adequately controlled for. These compounds, also known as glycotoxins, may contribute to the harmful effects of high-fat foods beyond the impact of oxidized fatty acids.
